title: Real-time fraud detection
like: card fraud checks at a bank
brief: Every card payment asks your system "is this fraud?" and wants the answer within about 150 milliseconds. Each check looks up the cardholder's recent habits and runs a model. The holiday shopping rush doubles the volume, and a bad model update can start declining honest customers.

clarify.q: How long do we have for the answer?
clarify.a: About 150 ms in total. The card network gives up soon after.

clarify.q: What if we are too slow?
clarify.a: The payment fails or is approved without a check, both of which cost money. Staying fast matters more than being perfect.

clarify.q: Where do the cardholder's habits come from?
clarify.a: A feature store of recent activity, updated by a stream of events as payments happen.

clarify.q: Can a new model go wrong?
clarify.a: Yes. Releases need a way back in seconds, because declined honest customers call the bank immediately.

notes: A "payment" here is one authorization check.
Analysts review flagged cases in a console.

hints: The model and the feature store are on the path of every payment. What happens to your servers when one of them gets slow?
Short timeouts and a circuit breaker keep a slow helper from freezing everything. A release pipeline with a quick rollback and a feature flag cover a bad model.

Servers call a feature store and a model server through a breaker, store the decision in a key-value store, and send events to a stream. Add CI/CD for rollbacks, feature flags, and alerting so someone knows within minutes.

editorial.summary: Two latency budgets decide this design: 150 ms for the whole check, and whatever the slowest helper takes. Short timeouts and a circuit breaker stop one slow helper from stalling thousands of servers. Headroom handles the holiday doubling because model servers take minutes to start. The model is deployed behind a pipeline with a canary and a kill switch, because the worst outage here is a wrong model, not a dead server.

designs.name: Fast checks, short timeouts, quick rollback
designs.why: Servers fetch features and a score in parallel hops measured in a few milliseconds. The hops run side by side and each gives up within 100 ms, and the feature store sits behind a breaker that gives up after 50 ms, so a sick helper costs a few fast failures and never the whole 150 ms budget. A key-value store keeps the decisions, and the release tools make a bad model a 30-second problem.

tradeoffs: A timeout must sit well inside the budget: with 150 ms for the whole check, hops that run side by side each give up within 50 to 100 ms. Some checks then fail fast when a helper is sick; the alternative is every server frozen waiting and the card network giving up first.

A circuit breaker in front of the decision store trades a short burst of fast failures for the whole fleet staying healthy, and the short timeouts do the same job for the model and the feature store. The business then decides what a failed check does: approve small amounts, decline large ones.
Model servers are provisioned for the holiday peak in advance. Autoscaling alone adds capacity after a minute of measuring plus boot time, and cards do not wait.
A canary release and a kill switch cost about $500 a month and cap a bad model's damage to minutes. Without them, a bad model can decline honest customers for an hour.
The feature store and key-value store add two hops to every check. Together they are about 8 ms in the same zone, well inside a 150 ms budget.
editorial.realWorld: Card fraud systems at large issuers score each authorization in a few tens of milliseconds, inside a total budget of about 100 to 150 ms, and retrain models regularly (approx.).
